To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) in the four economies considered, the exchange rate does not play an important role in shock-absorption; (ii) the exchange rate is not a source of shocks in Canada and the UK, but is in Sweden and Denmark; (iii) monetary union is a viable option for Sweden and Denmark but not for Canada or the UK.

• The UK, Canada and Sweden all appear to have been subject to shocks from the exchange rate, which have been amplified by monetary policy, in a manner that is not consistent with the notion of the exchange rate as an effective shock-absorber.
the exchange rate is a source of shocks in the UK and Canada but acts as a shock-absorber in Sweden and Denmark.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: what is the relationship between exchange rates and the business cycle?
the question of how far the exchange rate can be used as a source of stabilisation, and whether the exchange rate can also be a source of shocks.
a number of questions: 1) What are the sources of shocks to an economy?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the exchange rate can be a useful shock-absorber, but that it can also be a source of shocks.
the exchange rate can, in principle, be a useful shock absorber, but only if it is not used as a monetary policy target.
the exchange rate can be a shock-absorber, but only if the monetary authorities have a credible commitment to exchange rate stability.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the UK is the most open of the four countries studied, and that the UK is also most exposed to exchange market shocks.
a floating exchange rate may provide some shock-absorbing capacity, but not necessarily enough to offset the shock-absorbing potential of a credible monetary policy.
a monetary union is more likely to succeed if it is accompanied by fiscal union.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a monetary union is not a cure-all.
the monetary policy rule is the key to the effectiveness of a fixed exchange rate.
the exchange rate can act as a shock-absorber if monetary policy is conducted in an appropriate way.
